title: Can the Mother Nature Programme, a 6-week nature-based group programme for mothers experiencing low mood after having a baby and their babies, be tested in a larger randomised trial?
official: A randomised feasibility trial of a nature-based group intervention (the Mother Nature Programme) compared with usual care for mothers experiencing symptoms of postnatal depression and their infants
summary:
Background and study aims
Postnatal depression affects around one in ten mothers in the UK. It can make everyday life and caring for a baby much harder. Talking therapies and antidepressants can help, but many mothers find these difficult to access, or feel that they do not fit in with their lives or beliefs.
Spending time outdoors in nature can help many people with low mood, anxiety and stress, but we do not know whether it could help mothers with postnatal depression. Together with mothers who have experienced postnatal depression, we have developed the Mother Nature Programme. This is a 6-week outdoor group programme for mothers and their babies, with gentle activities in nature and time to connect with other mothers.
Before we run a larger study to find out whether the programme improves mental health and is good value for money, we need to know whether that study would be practical and acceptable to mothers. We will look at whether we can recruit mothers from a wide range of backgrounds, whether they are willing to be put into one of two groups by chance, whether they stay in the study, and whether the questionnaires and other study procedures work well for them.

Who can participate?
Mothers aged 16 years or over who have a baby under 12 months old when they join the study, are struggling with their mood, and are willing and able to attend an outdoor group with their baby if they are allocated to the programme. Mothers can take part if they also experience anxiety or are already receiving treatment for their mental health. They do not need a diagnosis of postnatal depression. Recruitment will take place in Bristol and Cornwall.
A short questionnaire and a conversation with the research team will help us check whether the study is suitable. Interpreter support and reasonable adjustments will be offered where available. The study may not be suitable for someone who currently needs urgent or inpatient mental health care.

What does the study involve?
We will recruit 48 mothers and their babies. After an initial assessment, mothers will be allocated by chance to one of two groups. Half will be offered the Mother Nature Programme (in groups of around six mother-baby pairs) alongside their usual care. The other half will continue with their usual care. Everyone will receive information about local NHS and community support.
The programme involves six weekly sessions, each lasting 2 hours, in local parks, community gardens and other green spaces. Mothers attend with their babies. Two trained facilitators lead gentle activities such as noticing sounds and textures, a slow wander, and creative or reflective activities. Mothers can choose whether to join in or share their experiences, and can respond to their babies’ needs throughout.
Everyone completes questionnaires at the start, around the time the programme ends, and three months later. These ask about mood, anxiety, wellbeing, quality of life, the relationship between mother and baby, connection with nature, and use of health and care services.
Some mothers who take part in the study, some mothers who decide not to take part, and the programme facilitators, will also be invited to share their experiences through optional interviews.

What are the possible benefits and risks of participating?
Mothers offered the programme may enjoy spending time outdoors with their baby and meeting other mothers. We do not yet know whether the programme improves postnatal mental health, and taking part may not provide a direct benefit. Whichever group they are in, everyone who takes part will be helping to shape future research and support for mothers with postnatal depression.
Some questions or discussions about mental health may feel upsetting. Participants can take breaks, skip questions, or stop taking part altogether, without giving a reason. Outdoor venues are checked for safety and accessibility, activities can be adapted, and sessions are changed or rescheduled if conditions are unsafe.
Taking part also involves time for questionnaires, appointments and, for those allocated to the programme, the sessions. Reasonable travel and childcare costs are reimbursed. Participants receive a £20 shopping voucher at each questionnaire assessment and an additional £20 voucher if they take part in an interview.
Usual care continues throughout, and choosing to stop taking part does not affect anyone’s access to their care.

Where is the study run from?
The University of Bristol (UK), with recruitment and the outdoor groups taking place in the Bristol and Cornwall regions.

When is the study starting and how long is it expected to run for?
The study is expected to run from January 2027 to December 2028. Recruitment is planned to last 18 months, with follow-up completed around 24 months after the first participant joins. Each mother takes part for around 6 months.

Who is funding the study?
The National Institute for Health and Care Research (NIHR) (UK), through a Doctoral Fellowship awarded to Dr Katherine Hall (NIHR304662).

Who is the main contact?
Mother Nature Programme research team, mother-nature-project@bristol.ac.uk

interventions.name:
This is an open-label, individually randomised feasibility trial involving 48 mothers and their infants. Following consent and baseline assessment, participants will be allocated in a 1:1 ratio to the Mother Nature Programme plus signposted usual care or signposted usual care alone.

Mother Nature P

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
1. Aged 16 years or over
2. Within 12 months postpartum at the point of consent
3. Score >=10 on the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale (EPDS), indicating possible or likely symptoms of postnatal depression (no formal diagnosis is required)
4. Willing to attend group sessions with their infant if randomised to the Mother Nature Programme intervention arm
5. Able to engage with the study and the intervention with the support of interpreters and/or translated materials available in the recruitment areas
Exclusion criteria:
1. Current postpartum psychosis, current or recent (within 12 months) mania or hypomania, untreated bipolar affective disorder, organic mental disorder, or substance dependence disorder, as judged by the participant’s usual clinician or the CI in consultation with the named clinical advisor
2. Current acute suicidality requiring crisis management
3. Judged by their clinician or the CI to pose a high risk to themselves or others, including their infant
4. Currently requiring admission, or planned admission, to a psychiatric inpatient unit (including a Mother and Baby Unit)
5. Active safeguarding concerns regarding the mother or infant where group participation at that time would not be appropriate, in the judgement of the CI in consultation with the relevant clinical or local safeguarding team
6. A physical health condition that would prevent safe participation in outdoor group activities and that cannot be addressed through reasonable adjustments
7. Language barriers that cannot be overcome through interpreter, translation or community support

Coexisting anxiety, antidepressant or other prescribed treatment use, and pregnancy during the study do not exclude participation.
